title: Bartholomew's Splashy Secret
markdown:
Bartholomew Bumble was a goat who felt quite a lot of pride. Not the show-off kind. His pride was a quiet, steady thing, like a strong root. He kept the prize-winning rose garden at Willow Creek Public Gardens, and those roses bloomed as if they had been written in red, pink, and yellow. Each soft petal showed how well he looked after them. He had a secret, though, a little knot of worry he kept hidden like a seed in winter. He could spot a plant disease from far away and trim a thorny stem with perfect care. There was one thing he disliked more than slugs on a young plant: being wrong. Especially in front of important people. It made his whiskers droop and his tail twitch.

His best friend, who helped when that pride got a bit too much, was Nell. Nell was a tortoise whose shell was the colour of old moss, with swirls that looked as if the wind had drawn them. She moved slowly, like the sun coming up. She understood Bartholomew’s pride. She knew it was a garden that needed a little sunshine, not a storm. “You worry too much, Barty,” she would say, her voice a soft rumble like pebbles in a dry creek.

“A gardener’s good name is as delicate as a butterfly’s wing,” Bartholomew would reply, fixing a rose leaf with his neat hoof. “One wrong word, one misplaced tool, and it is all ruined.” He would shudder, horns gleaming in the dappled light.

One bright Tuesday the garden office buzzed with hushed excitement. Bartholomew was pretending to study a ladybug when he heard the head gardener mumble. “Mr. Sterling, the important inspector, is coming this week. He’s seen gardens all over the place. If he likes our roses, it will be great for everyone.”

Bartholomew’s ears swivelled. Mr. Sterling! The same Mr. Sterling who had once, in a famously sharp voice, called a perfectly nice marigold a plain, not very exciting, bit of colour. A prickle of annoyance returned, stronger. This was his chance to show the garden at its best, and himself as someone who never made a mistake. He needed to look calm. Collected. A peaceful expert.

“Nell, my dear,” he announced, puffing out his chest and trying to look casual, though his eyes sparkled. “I think we need a special trip. To the Willow Creek Public Baths. A nice calm swim, to help me feel peaceful and in charge. A cool dip to smooth out any worries.”

Nell blinked slowly. “The baths, Barty? Are you sure that will help your roses? They do not seem to be wilting.”

“It will help me. A calm gardener does the best work. Mr. Sterling needs to see me as the most relaxed person. We must look amazing.” He practised a grand nod and almost tumbled over.

So Bartholomew Bumble, with neatly combed goat hair and a dab of rose-scented oil, trotted toward the sparkling blue baths. Nell followed, a quiet shadow of wisdom. He imagined himself gliding, graceful as a swan. He pictured Mr. Sterling nodding. Ah, what a calm person.

He stayed in the shallow end, of course. Deep water was too unpredictable. He dipped a hoof, then another, trying to move with the slow smooth style he thought inspectors would have. He even tried a little side stroke, which mostly meant wobbling and pretending not to notice his own awkward splashes. Nell found a sunny spot on a big fluffy towel and soaked up the warmth. Bartholomew was just beginning to feel a little confident when—

A child of about eight let out a happy yell and cannonballed into the water a few lanes away. The splash sent a huge wave toward Bartholomew. Cold water stung his eyes. His practised calm vanished like mist. He sputtered, flailed, and in a rather clumsy roll sent his precious gardening shears — he always carried them, in case a rose needed a quick trim — clattering onto the tiles.

And then he saw him. Standing by the edge, wiping his glasses with a clean white handkerchief, Mr. Sterling looked perfectly dry. A small amused smile touched his lips. Bartholomew felt his face turn a red that would have made his brightest roses look pale. The perfect gardener had just splashed about like a silly toy in front of the famous inspector.

He scrambled out, dripping, the rose-scented oil washing away. Nell walked toward him, her steady pace a comfort.

“Oh, Barty,” she said softly. “Sometimes it is better to be honest. Trying to be a graceful swan when you are a goat who just got splashed only makes it feel worse.”

Bartholomew hung his head. Wet fur stuck to him. “I wanted to impress him. I hate being wrong. I hate looking silly. I thought if I looked totally calm he would think I was the best gardener ever.”

Mr. Sterling walked over, his smile growing. “Mr. Bumble, I assume? That is a very interesting way you have of pruning in the water.” He chuckled, a warm real sound. “I have been trying to impress people with my garden since I was a kid. Real confidence is not about never making a mistake. It is about what you do when you do. And,” he winked, pointing to the wet shears, “a good laugh can solve more problems than a perfect petal. I once tried to look very calm before a big show by standing on my head. It did not end well. My marigolds, though, were amazing. Maybe you are just as tough with your own plants.”

Bartholomew looked at Mr. Sterling, then at Nell, who gave a slow encouraging nod, her shell shining. A weight lifted, better than any cold swim.

“Thank you, Mr. Sterling.” A small real smile appeared. It felt better than trying to look perfect. “I guess I have a lot to learn about being a truly great gardener. And about swimming baths.” He even managed a little laugh, wobbly but honest.

As Mr. Sterling walked away, waving his handkerchief at the man polishing the diving board, Bartholomew looked at his wet shears, then at Nell. He nudged her gently with his nose. The shears dripped onto the tiles, a small unexpected watering. Later, back among the roses, he hung them to dry on a hook and left a few drops on the nearest yellow bloom, as if the garden could use a splash that had not been on the plan.
characters: Bartholomew Bumble (observant goat gardener), Nell (tortoise friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
